text:
If two of your strongest engineers are in conflict and you let it run another quarter of quiet standoffs, the whole team will suffer. Google's Project Aristotle studied 180 teams and found that psychological safety mattered more than who was on the team.

Don't try to manage their personalities. Manage where their responsibilities meet. Most feuds between senior engineers are really disputes over who has authority over a design, even when they look personal. A document that sets out who decides what will usually cool much of the tension.

Meet with each engineer separately first. You'll likely find that each believes the other is slowing delivery. Then schedule a joint session with a written agenda and one shared, measurable deliverable. Tuckman's 1965 model calls this stage "storming", and teams that skip it rarely reach "performing".

Watch the comment threads on code reviews, because tension shows up in their tone before anyone resigns. If one of them threatens to leave, remember that replacing a senior engineer often costs six to nine months of salary. Step in early, because waiting until late may leave you no option except letting one of them go.
